span.label: SEVENTEEN DEFINITIONS AND TWELVE MODELS OF ONE CONSTRUCT, CONTENT-ANALYSED INTO SIX CLUSTERS AND THEN INTO ONE DEFINITION - the fourth procedure this corpus has seen applied to a contested term, after counting, voting, and refusing to choose
span.quote: The review resulted in 17 definitions of health literacy and 12 conceptual models. Based on the content analysis, an integrative conceptual model was developed containing 12 dimensions referring to the knowledge, motivation and competencies of accessing, understanding, appraising and applying health-related information within the healthcare, disease prevention and health promotion setting, respectively.

span.label: how health literacy is defined and how it can be conceptualised - and whether the diverging definitions can be integrated rather than adjudicated
span.quote: Although its importance is increasingly recognised, there is no consensus about the definition of health literacy or about its conceptual dimensions, which limits the possibilities for measurement and comparison. The aim of the study is to review definitions and models on health literacy to develop an integrated definition and conceptual model capturing the most comprehensive evidence-based dimensions of health literacy.

span.label: an `all inclusive` definition condensed from 17, and an integrated model yielding 12 dimensions as the product of four competencies and three health domains
span.quote: Health literacy is linked to literacy and entails people's knowledge, motivation and competences to access, understand, appraise, and apply health information in order to make judgments and take decisions in everyday life concerning healthcare, disease prevention and health promotion to maintain or improve quality of life during the life course . This definition encompasses the public health perspective and can easily be specified to accommodate an individual approach by substituting the three domains of health "healthcare, disease prevention and health promotion" with "being ill, being at risk and staying healthy".

span.label: method
span.quote: The content analysis on the definitions yielded six clusters representing: (1) competence, skills, abilities; (2) actions; (3) information and resources; (4) objective; (5) context; and (6) time as outlined in Table 2 . Accordingly each cluster was carefully examined, discussed and condensed by the research team and the resulting chosen terms and notions were combined to yield a new 'all inclusive' comprehensive definition capturing the essence of the 17 definitions identified in the literature:

span.label: a construct with nearly 5,000 publications, an EU policy priority and no agreed definition, whose measurement tools do not capture what its literature describes
span.quote: However, with the proliferation of health literacy research and policy measures, it becomes clear that there is no unanimously accepted definition of the concept. Moreover, the constituent dimensions of health literacy remain disputed, and attempts to operationalize the concept vary widely in scope, method and quality. As a result, it is very difficult to compare findings with regard to health literacy emerging from research in different countries.

span.label: a systematic review in Medline, Pubmed and Web of Science by two independent teams, then a three-step content analysis: coding by both teams separately, discussion with a European expert panel, and a final integration by the original team

span.label: **THE FOURTH PROCEDURE, AND THE CORPUS HAD NO INSTANCE OF IT**: `The review resulted in 17 DEFINITIONS of health literacy and 12 CONCEPTUAL MODELS. Based on the content analysis, AN INTEGRATIVE CONCEPTUAL MODEL WAS DEVELOPED CONTAINING 12 DIMENSIONS.` Reviews that COUNT definitions, bodies that VOTE on one, a panel that REFUSES TO CHOOSE - and now one that **SYNTHESISES**: seventeen go in, six clusters come out of the content analysis, one definition comes out of the clusters
span.quote: The review resulted in 17 definitions of health literacy and 12 conceptual models. Based on the content analysis, an integrative conceptual model was developed containing 12 dimensions referring to the knowledge, motivation and competencies of accessing, understanding, appraising and applying health-related information within the healthcare, disease prevention and health promotion setting, respectively.

span.label: AND THE SIX CLUSTERS ARE THE AXES OF THE SYNTHESIS: `The content analysis on the definitions yielded six clusters representing: (1) COMPETENCE, SKILLS, ABILITIES; (2) ACTIONS; (3) INFORMATION AND RESOURCES; (4) OBJECTIVE; (5) CONTEXT; and (6) TIME.` Each cluster `carefully examined, discussed and condensed by the research team` - so the output definition is a sentence assembled slot by slot from what the seventeen had in common
span.quote: The content analysis on the definitions yielded six clusters representing: (1) competence, skills, abilities; (2) actions; (3) information and resources; (4) objective; (5) context; and (6) time as outlined in Table 2 . Accordingly each cluster was carefully examined, discussed and condensed by the research team and the resulting chosen terms and notions were combined to yield a new 'all inclusive' comprehensive definition capturing the essence of the 17 definitions identified in the literature:

span.label: **AND THE RESULTING DEFINITION SHIPS WITH A SUBSTITUTION RULE FOR CHANGING ITS PERSPECTIVE**: `Health literacy is linked to literacy and entails people's KNOWLEDGE, MOTIVATION AND COMPETENCES TO ACCESS, UNDERSTAND, APPRAISE, AND APPLY HEALTH INFORMATION ... This definition encompasses the public health perspective and CAN EASILY BE SPECIFIED TO ACCOMMODATE AN INDIVIDUAL APPROACH BY SUBSTITUTING the three domains of health `healthcare, disease prevention and health promotion` WITH `being ill, being at risk and staying healthy`.` nakagawa2017 printed a substitution table for a statistic's NAME; **this prints one for a definition's SCOPE**
span.quote: Health literacy is linked to literacy and entails people's knowledge, motivation and competences to access, understand, appraise, and apply health information in order to make judgments and take decisions in everyday life concerning healthcare, disease prevention and health promotion to maintain or improve quality of life during the life course . This definition encompasses the public health perspective and can easily be specified to accommodate an individual approach by substituting the three domains of health "healthcare, disease prevention and health promotion" with "being ill, being at risk and staying healthy".

span.label: **AND THE TWELVE DIMENSIONS ARE A PRODUCT, NOT A DISCOVERY**: `THE COMBINATION OF THE FOUR DIMENSIONS referring to health information processing WITH THE THREE LEVELS OF DOMAINS YIELDS A MATRIX WITH 12 DIMENSIONS of health literacy.` Four times three. The count in the abstract, the conclusion and every citing paper is the size of a grid, and the grid is filled by construction rather than by observation
span.quote: The combination of the four dimensions referring to health information processing with the three levels of domains yields a matrix with 12 dimensions of health literacy as illustrated in Table 4 .

span.label: AND THE FOUR COMPETENCIES ARE A PIPELINE, EACH WITH ITS OWN FAILURE MODE: `(1) ACCESS refers to the ability to seek, find and obtain health information; (2) UNDERSTAND ...; (3) APPRAISE describes the ability to interpret, filter, judge and evaluate ...; and (4) APPLY refers to the ability to communicate and use the information to make a decision.` And each `DEPENDS ON THE QUALITY OF THE INFORMATION PROVIDED` - so a competence attributed to a person is partly a property of the documents they were handed
span.quote: The core of the model shows the competencies related to the process of accessing, understanding, appraising and applying health-related information. According to the 'all inclusive' definition this process requires four types of competencies: (1) Access refers to the ability to seek, find and obtain health information; (2) Understand refers to the ability to comprehend the health information that is accessed; (3) Appraise describes the ability to interpret, filter, judge and evaluate the health information that has been accessed; and (4) Apply refers to the ability to communicate and use the information to make a decision to maintain and improve health.

span.label: **AND THE MODEL WILL BE VALIDATED BY THE INSTRUMENT BUILT FROM IT**: `As currently available tools to measure health literacy DO NOT CAPTURE ALL ASPECTS OF THE CONCEPT ... scales can be developed to assess the dimensions outlined in the conceptual model presented in this paper. This will not only produce a comprehensive measure ... BUT ALSO SERVE TO VALIDATE THE CONCEPTUAL MODEL and thus contribute to the understanding of health literacy.` The circularity is stated openly and without embarrassment, in the conclusion
span.quote: As currently available tools to measure health literacy do not capture all aspects of the concept as discussed in the literature, there is a need to develop new tools to assess health literacy, reflecting health literacy definitions and accompanying conceptual models for public health. By following a concept validation approach, scales can be developed to assess the dimensions outlined in the conceptual model presented in this paper. This will not only produce a comprehensive measure of health literacy, reflecting the state of the art of the field and applicable for social research and in public health practice, but also serve to validate the conceptual model and thus contribute to the understanding of health literacy.

span.label: AND ONE TRADITION CARRIES THREE NAMES AND THE OTHER ONE: `The first is referred to as `MEDICAL HEALTH LITERACY`, `PATIENT HEALTH LITERACY`, or `CLINICAL HEALTH LITERACY`; the second as `PUBLIC HEALTH LITERACY`. Nutbeam refers to THE OPPOSING medical and public health views ... as respectively a `CLINICAL RISK`, and a `PERSONAL ASSET` approach, and points out that they are ROOTED IN THE DIFFERENT TRADITIONS of clinical care, and adult learning and health promotion.` **The same word names a risk to be screened for and an asset to be built**
span.quote: One perspective is that they refer to a series of individual cognitive skills and abilities applied in a medical context; the other perspective sees a broader range of competencies applied in the social realm. The first is referred to as "medical health literacy" [ 5 ], "patient health literacy" [ 14 ], or "clinical health literacy" [ 63 ]; the second as "public health literacy" [ 35 ]. Nutbeam [ 52 ] refers to the opposing medical and public health views on health literacy as respectively a "clinical risk", and a "personal asset" approach, and points out that they are rooted in the different traditions of clinical care, and adult learning and health promotion, respectively. As both perspectives are important and useful to enable a better understanding of health communication processes in clinical and community settings, any definition of health literacy needs to integrate both views.

span.label: AND THE FIVE SHORTCOMINGS OF THE EXISTING MODELS ARE ENUMERATED BEFORE THE NEW ONE IS OFFERED: `FIRSTLY, most of the existing conceptual models ARE NOT SUFFICIENTLY GROUNDED IN THEORY ... SECONDLY, VERY FEW MODELS HAVE INTEGRATED the components included in `medical` and `public health` literacy models ... THIRDLY ... the majority of the existing models ARE RATHER STATIC and do not explicitly account for the fact that health literacy is also A PROCESS ... FOURTHLY ... THE PATHWAYS ... ARE NOT VERY CLEAR` - and fifthly, `VERY FEW ... HAVE BEEN EMPIRICALLY VALIDATED`
span.quote: Firstly, most of the existing conceptual models are not sufficiently grounded in theory in terms of the notions and concepts included. Secondly, very few models have integrated the components included in "medical" and "public health" literacy models. The only models which explicitly try to bridge the difference between both views are Nutbeam's [ 36 ] and Manganello's [ 50 ], whose dimension of functional literacy corresponds with the cognitive skills of medical health literacy. Thirdly, while acknowledging that health literacy entails different dimensions, the majority of the existing models are rather static and do not explicitly account for the fact that health literacy is also a process, which involves the consecutive steps of accessing, understanding, processing and communicating information. Fourthly, while most conceptual models identify the factors that influence health literacy and mention its impact on health service use, health costs and health outcomes, the pathways linking health literacy to its antecedents and consequences are not very clear.

span.label: AND THE CHARGE THAT THE WHOLE CONSTRUCT IS REDUNDANT IS QUOTED, NOT SUPPRESSED: `Although some authors have argued that health literacy is merely `NEW WINE IN OLD BOTTLES`, and is basically THE REPACKAGING OF CONCEPTS CENTRAL TO THE IDEOLOGICAL THEORY AND PRACTICE OF HEALTH PROMOTION, enhancing health literacy is increasingly recognized as a public health goal.` The objection is answered by adoption rather than by argument
span.quote: Although some authors have argued that health literacy is merely "new wine in old bottles", and is basically the repackaging of concepts central to the ideological theory and practice of health promotion [ 64 ], enhancing health literacy is increasingly recognized as a public health goal and a determinant of health.

span.label: AND THE PARENT TERM IS SEPARATED FROM THE CHILD ONE EXPLICITLY: `IT IS IMPORTANT TO DISTINGUISH HEALTH LITERACY FROM LITERACY IN GENERAL. According to ... UNESCO ... the word `literate` mostly meant to be `FAMILIAR WITH LITERATURE` or in general terms `WELL EDUCATED, LEARNED` ... during the late nineteenth century IT HAS ALSO COME TO REFER TO THE ABILITIES TO READ AND WRITE TEXT.` The compound is defined against a head noun whose own sense moved in the nineteenth century
span.quote: It is important to distinguish health literacy from literacy in general. According to the United Nation Education, Science and Culture Organization (UNESCO) during its history in English, the word 'literate' mostly meant to be 'familiar with literature' or in general terms 'well educated, learned'. While maintaining its broader meaning of being knowledgeable or educated in a particular area, during the late nineteenth century it has also come to refer to the abilities to read and write text.

span.label: AND THE RELATIONSHIP TO OUTCOMES IS A STEP FUNCTION, NOT A LINE: `The relationship of health literacy to health outcomes according to these authors MUST BE CONCEIVED AS A STEP FUNCTION WITH A THRESHOLD EFFECT, RATHER THAN IN A SIMPLE LINEAR FASHION. People generally exist within a web of social relationships; and BELOW A CERTAIN LEVEL OF FUNCTION, much of the day-to-day detail of chronic disease management OFTEN NEEDS TO BE FACILITATED BY OTHERS.` A construct measured on an individual whose consequences depend on who else is in the room
span.quote: The relationship of health literacy to health outcomes according to these authors must be conceived as a step function with a threshold effect, rather than in a simple linear fashion. People generally exist within a web of social relationships; and below a certain level of function, much of the day-to-day detail of chronic disease management often needs to be facilitated by others. While the interaction between health literacy and social support is likely to have complicated and subtle implications, the health impact of social effects has not been fully elucidated in the context of health literacy [ 54 ].

span.label: AND THE FIELD IS BIG, YOUNG AND UNEVEN: `The research literature on health literacy has EXPANDED EXPONENTIALLY, with NEARLY 5,000 PubMed-listed publications to date ... THE MAJORITY OF WHICH HAVE BEEN PUBLISHED SINCE 2005`, spread across health educators, lawyers, communication, prevalence studies and empowerment work. The term was `INTRODUCED IN THE 1970s`, so the definitional disagreement is forty years old and the literature that carries it is mostly seven
span.quote: The research literature on health literacy has expanded exponentially, with nearly 5,000 PubMed-listed publications to date (Primo November 2011), the majority of which have been published since 2005 [ 5 , 14 ] and is evident that health literacy is being explored within different disciplines and with different approaches, e.g. looking at the role of health educators in promoting health literacy [ 15 ]; public health literacy for lawyers [ 16 ], health communication [ 17 ], the prevalence of limited health literacy [ 18 ], and health literacy as an empowerment tool for low-income mothers [ 19 ].

span.label: SEVENTEEN DEFINITIONS AND TWELVE MODELS, COUNTED: `The review resulted in 17 DEFINITIONS of health literacy and 12 CONCEPTUAL MODELS.` Table 1 prints them with their owners - WHO (1998), the American Medical Association, the Institute of Medicine - so the disagreement is enumerated and attributed rather than described.
span.quote: The review resulted in 17 definitions of health literacy and 12 conceptual models

span.label: AND THE REPAIR IS A FOURTH KIND, NOT SEEN ELSEWHERE IN THIS CORPUS: `A CONTENT ANALYSIS OF THE DEFINITIONS and conceptual frameworks WAS CARRIED OUT to identify the central dimensions of health literacy and DEVELOP AN INTEGRATED MODEL.` The competing definitions are not adjudicated, refused, or handed to a committee - THEY ARE TREATED AS DATA AND ANALYSED, and what comes out is twelve dimensions rather than a winner.
span.quote: A content analysis of the definitions and conceptual frameworks was carried out to identify the central dimensions of health literacy and develop an integrated model

span.label: AND THE YIELD IS SMALLER THAN THE SEARCH: `From the 19 publications FOCUSING SPECIFICALLY ON DEFINITIONS of health literacy, 17 EXPLICIT DEFINITIONS COULD BE DERIVED.` Two papers about the definition of a term did not contain one that could be extracted.
span.quote: From the 19 publications focusing specifically on definitions of health literacy 17 explicit definitions could be derived

span.label: **THE MODELS BEING INTEGRATED HAVE MOSTLY NEVER BEEN TESTED**: `Researchers could link conceptual models of health literacy more explicitly to established health promotion theories and models. Finally, VERY FEW CONCEPTUAL MODELS OF HEALTH LITERACY HAVE BEEN EMPIRICALLY VALIDATED.` The synthesis inherits whatever is wrong with its twelve inputs, and the paper says the inputs are untested
span.quote: Researchers could link conceptual models of health literacy more explicitly to established health promotion theories and models [ 59 ]. Finally, very few conceptual models of health literacy have been empirically validated.

span.label: AND NONE OF THE EXISTING MODELS IS ADEQUATE, WHICH IS THE PREMISE: `Whereas a number of conceptual models ... have been presented in the literature, NONE OF THESE CAN BE REGARDED AS SUFFICIENTLY COMPREHENSIVE to line up with the evolving health literacy definitions and with the competencies they imply. This is probably due to the fact that attempts to conceptualize health literacy HAVE THUS FAR FAILED TO INTEGRATE THE EXISTING KNOWLEDGE.` The new model's warrant is the inadequacy of the twelve it is built from
span.quote: Whereas a number of conceptual models of health literacy have been presented in the literature, none of these can be regarded as sufficiently comprehensive to line up with the evolving health literacy definitions and with the competencies they imply [ 59 ]. This is probably due to the fact that attempts to conceptualize health literacy have thus far failed to integrate the existing knowledge encompassing different perspectives on health literacy.

span.label: AND THE WHOLE DIVERSITY IS THEN REDUCED TO TWO AXES: `the range of factors that are considered as key components of health literacy is EXTENSIVE, and there is A WIDE VARIATION BETWEEN CONCEPTUAL MODELS. However, THIS DIVERSITY OF VIEWS CAN TO A LARGE EXTENT BE REDUCED TO TWO DIMENSIONS, notably THE CORE QUALITIES of health literacy ... and ITS SCOPE AND AREA OF APPLICATION.` Twelve models collapse to two axes and then expand to a twelve-cell grid - and the two twelves are not the same twelve
span.quote: In conclusion, the range of factors that are considered as key components of health literacy is extensive, and there is a wide variation between conceptual models. However, this diversity of views can to a large extent be reduced to two dimensions, notably the core qualities of health literacy (e.g., basic or functional, interactive, and critical health literacy), and its scope and area of application (e.g., as a patient in healthcare, as a consumer at the market, as a citizen in the political arena, or as a member of the audience in relation to the media).

span.label: AND THE CONSEQUENCE OF NO AGREED DEFINITION IS STATED AS THE MOTIVE: `with the proliferation of health literacy research and policy measures, it becomes clear that THERE IS NO UNANIMOUSLY ACCEPTED DEFINITION of the concept. Moreover, THE CONSTITUENT DIMENSIONS ... REMAIN DISPUTED, and attempts to operationalize the concept VARY WIDELY IN SCOPE, METHOD AND QUALITY. As a result, IT IS VERY DIFFICULT TO COMPARE FINDINGS ... FROM RESEARCH IN DIFFERENT COUNTRIES.` The cost of the disagreement is comparability, named in one sentence
span.quote: However, with the proliferation of health literacy research and policy measures, it becomes clear that there is no unanimously accepted definition of the concept. Moreover, the constituent dimensions of health literacy remain disputed, and attempts to operationalize the concept vary widely in scope, method and quality. As a result, it is very difficult to compare findings with regard to health literacy emerging from research in different countries.

At an individual level, ineffective communication due to poor health literacy will result in errors, poor quality, and risks to patient safety of the healthcare services [ 61 ].

span.quote: The prototypical model is that of Nutbeam [ 36 ], which distinguishes between three typologies of health literacy: (1) Functional health literacy refers to the basic skills in reading and writing that are necessary to function effectively in everyday situations, broadly comparable with the content of "medical" health literacy referred to above; (2) Interactive health literacy refers to more advanced cognitive and literacy skills which, together with social skills, can be used to actively participate in everyday situations, extract information and derive meaning from different forms of communication, and apply this to changing circumstance; and (3) Critical health literacy refers to more advanced cognitive skills which, together with social skills, can be applied to critically analyze information and use this to exert greater control over life events and situations.

span.label: critiques → the twelve existing conceptual models, `NONE OF [WHICH] CAN BE REGARDED AS SUFFICIENTLY COMPREHENSIVE`, on five enumerated grounds
span.quote: Firstly, most of the existing conceptual models are not sufficiently grounded in theory in terms of the notions and concepts included. Secondly, very few models have integrated the components included in "medical" and "public health" literacy models. The only models which explicitly try to bridge the difference between both views are Nutbeam's [ 36 ] and Manganello's [ 50 ], whose dimension of functional literacy corresponds with the cognitive skills of medical health literacy. Thirdly, while acknowledging that health literacy entails different dimensions, the majority of the existing models are rather static and do not explicitly account for the fact that health literacy is also a process, which involves the consecutive steps of accessing, understanding, processing and communicating information. Fourthly, while most conceptual models identify the factors that influence health literacy and mention its impact on health service use, health costs and health outcomes, the pathways linking health literacy to its antecedents and consequences are not very clear.

span.quote: The relationship of health literacy to health outcomes according to these authors must be conceived as a step function with a threshold effect, rather than in a simple linear fashion. While the interaction between health literacy and social support is likely to have complicated and subtle implications, the health impact of social effects has not been fully elucidated in the context of health literacy [ 54 ].

span.quote: The core of the model shows the competencies related to the process of accessing, understanding, appraising and applying health-related information. According to the 'all inclusive' definition this process requires four types of competencies: (1) Access refers to the ability to seek, find and obtain health information; (2) Understand refers to the ability to comprehend the health information that is accessed; (3) Appraise describes the ability to interpret, filter, judge and evaluate the health information that has been accessed; and (4) Apply refers to the ability to communicate and use the information to make a decision to maintain and improve health.
